queries.hook: The terror of a deadline that can take everything you built, and the mind that will not stop checking for proof that it is still safe.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse.sanskrit: सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति । वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते ॥ गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते । न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः ॥
verse.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.
verse.why: Even the strongest people freeze; the Gita begins with a breakdown, not a hero.
verse.misuse: Not a dismissal of anxiety; it shows that even the strong feel it, and the teaching starts there.

prasang.title: Overcome by delusion, Arjuna speaks in fear, love and grief
prasang.summary: Seeing his kin ready to die, Arjuna trembles, his bow slips, and he argues that no victory is worth killing family. He sits down in the chariot and refuses to fight.
prasang.story_hook: The greatest archer of his age stood between two armies, and his hands began to shake.
prasang.lesson: Even the strongest people freeze; the Gita begins with a breakdown, not a hero.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands in his chariot and sees his own kin arrayed against him. His limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. He is not a hero here. He is a man in the middle of a breakdown, and the Gita opens with that trembling, not with a command to be brave.
verse.for_you: You are checking messages at two in the morning because something in you is already bracing for the worst. The terror you feel is real, and it is not a failure of yours. It is simply the body telling the truth about what is at stake.

verse.speaker: Janaka
verse.setting: Janaka, having chosen to keep ruling, talks gently to his own restless mind at night.
verse.sanskrit: यथा यथा विकल्पौघान्संकल्पयसि हेलया । तथा तथैति स्फारत्वं संसारस्तव चिन्तया ॥
verse.line: The more scenarios you spin, the bigger your world of worry grows.
verse.translation: The more you casually spin up fancies and possibilities, the more your world of troubles swells, through your own worrying.
verse.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.meaning: King Janaka sits on his palace roof at night, questioning the life he has lived. He has heard the sages speak of a self that cannot be lost. He knows his duties wait below, but his mind is spinning with what might go wrong. He speaks to his own restlessness, telling it that the more fancies it spins, the larger his world of trouble becomes. The verse asks him to do his day's work, not by leaving his life, but by doing it with a mind that no longer clutches.
verse.for_you: Your mind is spinning scenarios about a rating that has not arrived yet. It is making the work itself feel like an enemy. The verse shows you a different way to meet the day. You do not have to leave your job to find peace.

verse.line: In loss, money trouble or fear, the steady person thinks it through and does not go under.
verse.translation: In disaster, in money trouble, in fear, even when life itself is at stake, the steady person who thinks things through with their own mind does not sink.
verse.why: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

prasang.title: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

verse.meaning: Lakshman speaks to Ram after Sita is taken. Ram is lost in grief and wants to destroy the world. Lakshman tells him to take heart. He asks which living being trouble does not touch. He says troubles strike like fire, king, and pass in a moment. A steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.
verse.for_you: The visa feels like a fire that will burn everything. But your mind is not the visa. It is the steady thing inside you that trouble cannot touch. That part of you cannot be lost.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: परिभ्रमसि किं मुधा क्वचन चित्त विश्राम्यतां स्वयं भवति यद्यथा भवति तत्तथा नान्यथा । अतीतमननुस्मरन्नपि च भाव्यसंकल्पयन् नतर्कितसमागमाननुभवामि भोगानहम् ॥
verse.line: Why wander, mind? Rest. Not replaying the past, not scripting the future, I take what comes.
verse.translation: Why do you wander about in vain, mind? Rest somewhere. Whatever is to happen happens just as it will, and not otherwise. Not recalling the past, not planning the future, I enjoy the pleasures that come to me unlooked-for.
verse.why: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.
verse.misuse: Not an argument against planning; it is for the worry loop once you have done your part.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasang.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasang.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to his own mind from a place of exhaustion. He asks why it wanders about in vain, why it replays the past and scripts the future. He says rest somewhere. Whatever is to happen will happen just as it will. He will not recall the past, will not plan the future, but will enjoy what comes unlooked-for. This is a voice that has already done its part and is now telling the mind to stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes. The calm is already inside.
verse.for_you: The rating will be what it is. You have already done what you can. Before dawn, turn the phone face down and let the night belong to rest.

verse.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
verse.translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the self.

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

verse.meaning: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to settle the mind. He describes a mind that wanders like a flame in the wind. The instruction is to bring it back to the self, again and again. script: You are terrified and running on empty. The visa, the rating, the sixty days. You check messages at two in the morning because sleep feels like a risk you cannot afford to take right now.

Arjuna stands in his chariot and sees his own kin arrayed against him. His limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. He is not a hero here. He is a man in the middle of a breakdown, and the Gita opens with that trembling, not with a command to be brave: And Arjuna said:
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति, वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते. गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते, न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः.
In plain words: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.

This is what it means to be strong. The body does not lie. It shakes and dries and races when the mind has already decided the worst is coming. The texts do not ask you to ignore this. They start exactly here, in the shaking. The fear of what might happen is real, and it is not a flaw in you. It is the ground you are standing on right now.
When the phone lights up at two in the morning, let your hand move slowly. Let the message sit for a breath before you read it. Your body is already bracing for a loss it cannot control.
The tremor is not the end of you.

depth.points: The Gita begins with a waves of panic. Even the strongest freeze. The body is not failing. It is telling the truth about what is at stake. Fear of what might happen is real, and it is the ground the teaching starts from.
depth.practice: Notice one sensation in the body right now without trying to change it.
depth.question: What does your body know right now that your mind is trying to ignore?
